title: Key Characteristics of Distributed Systems
summary: The fundamental properties that define distributed systems — scalability, availability, reliability, consistency, and the trade-offs between them.

explanation.overview: A distributed system is a collection of independent computers that appear to users as a single coherent system. Every large-scale application (Google, Netflix, Amazon) is a distributed system. Understanding the key characteristics helps you make informed design decisions — every architecture is a set of trade-offs among these properties. DEVELOPER BLOG INSIGHT: 'Jumping from monolithic to distributed systems is like jumping from an acoustic guitar to a full symphony orchestra in a hurricane.' ## Performance vs scalability A service is **scalable** if it results in increased **performance** in a manner proportional to resources added. Generally, increasing performance means serving more units of work, but it can also be to handle larger units of work, such as when datasets grow.1 Another way to look at performance vs scalability: * If you have a **performance** problem, your system is slow for a single user. * If you have a **scalability** problem, your system is fast for a single user but slow under heavy load. ### Source(s) and further reading * [A word on scalability](http://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2006/03/a_word_on_scalability.html) * [Scalability, availability, stability, patterns](http://www.slideshare.net/jboner/scalability-availability-stability-patterns/) ## Latency vs throughput **Latency** is the time to perform some action or to produce some result. **Throughput** is the number of such actions or results per unit of time. Generally, you should aim for **maximal throughput** with **acceptable latency**. ### Source(s) and further reading * [Understanding latency vs throughput](https://community.cadence.com/cadence_blogs_8/b/fv/posts/understanding-latency-vs-throughput)
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Distributed systems face challenges that monolithic systems don't: network is unreliable (packets drop, latency spikes), clocks are unsynchronized (each machine has slightly different time), nodes fail independently (one server crashes while others continue), and there's no shared memory (data must be explicitly communicated). These realities force you to make design trade-offs at every layer.

limitations: Network Unreliability: The Fallacies of Distributed Computing state the network is never 100% reliable. You must code for latency spikes, partitions, and dropped packets.
Increased Observability Overhead: When a request traverses 15 microservices, finding which one failed requires distributed tracing (Jaeger, Zipkin) and centralized logging (ELK).
Data Consistency: Unlike a monolithic SQL database, enforcing ACID guarantees across multiple geographic regions is mathematically impossible without sacrificing availability (CAP Theorem).
common_mistakes: Assuming zero latency between internal microservices.
Failing to implement Circuit Breakers (like Resilience4j or PyBreaker) when talking to downstream dependencies.
Using distributed systems when a monolithic Postgres instance and a simple state API would suffice (YAGNI).

children.title: Scalability
children.summary: The ability of a system to handle increasing load by adding resources.

explanation.overview: Scalability is the system's capacity to cope with increased demand. A scalable system maintains performance (latency, throughput) as load grows — more users, more data, more requests.

key_concepts.definition: INTERNAL: Add more resources to a single machine — more CPU, RAM, SSD, faster network. EXAMPLE: upgrade from 16 GB RAM to 128 GB, or 4-core to 64-core CPU. PROS: simple (no code changes), no distributed system complexity, data consistency is easy (single machine). CONS: hardware limits (you can't buy a machine with 100 TB RAM), cost grows exponentially (a 64-core server costs more than 16× a 4-core), single point of failure (if this machine dies, everything dies). INDUSTRY USE: databases often scale vertically first — a beefier Postgres server can handle a lot more before you need sharding. Amazon RDS instances go up to 24 TB RAM and 128 vCPUs.

Add more machines to the pool. Each machine handles a portion of the load. EXAMPLE: instead of 1 server handling 10K QPS, use 10 servers each handling 1K QPS behind a load balancer. PROS: practically unlimited scale (just add more machines), fault tolerant (one machine fails, others continue), cost-effective (commodity hardware). CONS: code must be stateless (or state must be externalized to a shared store like Redis), distributed systems complexity (data partitioning, replication, consistency), network communication overhead. INDUSTRY STANDARD: application servers should ALWAYS be designed for horizontal scaling from day one. Store all state in databases/caches, make servers stateless, put a load balancer in front.

The ability to automatically add or remove resources based on current demand. Cloud auto-scaling: AWS Auto Scaling Groups monitor CPU/memory metrics and add/remove EC2 instances. Kubernetes HPA (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler) adjusts pod count based on CPU or custom metrics. CONFIGURABLE: min instances (floor — always running), max instances (ceiling — cost control), scaling metric (CPU > 70%, QPS > 1000, queue depth > 100), cooldown period (wait 300s after scaling before evaluating again, prevents oscillation). EDGE CASE: cold start — new instances take time to boot, load code, warm caches. During traffic spikes, there's a lag between the spike and the new capacity. FIX: keep a buffer of warm standby instances, or use provisioned capacity.

examples.title: Netflix Scaling Pattern
examples.description: Netflix serves 250M+ subscribers. Their microservices (100+) run on thousands of EC2 instances with auto-scaling. During peak hours (8-11 PM), auto-scaling adds instances. At 3 AM, it removes them. Databases use a mix: Aurora (relational, vertically scaled up to db.r5.24xlarge) for user accounts, Cassandra (horizontally scaled, 1000+ nodes) for viewing history/recommendations.

examples.code:
try-catch fallback mechanics:
1. NetworkTimeoutException: Trigger circuit breaker and return stale cached data.
2. ConnectionRefusedException: Shift traffic to the standby region (Pilot Light architecture).
3. OOMError: Restart exact instance via Kubernetes Health Probes.

children.title: Availability
children.summary: The percentage of time a system is operational and accessible.

explanation.overview: Availability = uptime / (uptime + downtime). It's usually expressed as 'nines': 99% (two nines) = 3.65 days downtime/year. 99.9% (three nines) = 8.76 hours. 99.99% (four nines) = 52.6 minutes. 99.999% (five nines) = 5.26 minutes.
explanation.how_it_works_internally: Achieving high availability requires eliminating single points of failure (SPOF) at every layer. For each component, ask: 'if this dies, does the system stop working?' If yes, add redundancy. Load Balancer SPOF: deploy 2 LBs with floating IP (VIP) and keepalived/VRRP failover. App Server SPOF: run N instances behind LB; N-1 can handle full load. Database SPOF: primary + synchronous standby replica with automatic failover (Patroni for Postgres, RDS Multi-AZ). Cache SPOF: Redis Sentinel or Cluster mode for auto-failover. DNS SPOF: use multiple DNS providers (Cloudflare + Route 53).

key_concepts.definition: SLI (Service Level Indicator): the actual measurement (e.g., request success rate = 99.95% this month). SLO (Service Level Objective): the target (e.g., 'availability must be ≥ 99.9%'). SLA (Service Level Agreement): the contract with customers (e.g., 'if availability drops below 99.9%, customer gets service credits'). Google's SRE book: alert when burning through your error budget too fast, not on individual incidents.

Components in series (sequential dependency): overall = A1 × A2 × A3. If each is 99.9%, overall = 99.7%. Components in parallel (redundant): overall = 1 - (1-A1)(1-A2). Two 99.9% components in parallel = 1 - 0.001² = 99.9999%. IMPLICATION: minimize sequential dependencies (reduce the critical path). Add redundancy (parallel components) for each critical component.

Active-Passive (warm standby): primary handles traffic, standby replicates data. On primary failure, standby takes over (seconds to minutes). Active-Active: both nodes serve traffic simultaneously. On failure of one, the other absorbs its load. More complex (must handle conflicts) but zero-downtime failover. Multi-Region Active-Active: deploy in 2+ AWS regions. Route 53 health checks route traffic away from unhealthy regions automatically. This is how AWS, Google, and Netflix achieve five nines.

examples.title: AWS DynamoDB Outage Case Study (Cascading Failure)
examples.description: A textbook example of how a failure in a foundational service (DNS/Metadata) can cascade and take down a global distributed database.
examples.code:
What Happened:
An underlying sub-system responsible for metadata and DNS management experienced a latent race condition. When a network partition occurred, nodes began heavily querying the DNS management system to re-establish topology.

The Cascade:
The overwhelming query volume overwhelmed the metadata service, causing it to drop requests. Because nodes couldn't get metadata, they assumed more nodes had failed, sending EVEN MORE metadata requests. This recursive retry loop acts as a self-inflicted Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack.

Takeaway for Interviews:
Always discuss 'Thundering Herds' and Cascading Failures. The fix is to implement strict Circuit Breakers and Exponential Backoff + Jitter on all internal inter-service retries.

children.title: Reliability & Fault Tolerance
children.summary: The ability of a system to continue functioning correctly even when components fail.

explanation.overview: Reliability means the system performs its intended function correctly under stated conditions for a specified period. Fault tolerance is a subset — continuing to operate (possibly at degraded capacity) when components fail. The key insight: failures are inevitable at scale. With 10,000 servers, several fail every day. A reliable system is designed EXPECTING failure.

key_concepts.definition: MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures): average time between system failures. MTTR (Mean Time To Repair): average time to restore service after failure. Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). To improve availability, either increase MTBF (better hardware, redundancy) or decrease MTTR (automation, runbooks, observability). Netflix philosophy: focus on reducing MTTR rather than preventing all failures.

Active redundancy: multiple components active simultaneously (RAID-1 disk mirroring, load-balanced servers). Passive redundancy: standby component activated on failure (hot standby database). No redundancy: if it fails, feature is unavailable (acceptable for non-critical features like 'Related Products' on Amazon — main purchase flow still works).

Intentionally inject failures in production to verify the system recovers correctly. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production EC2 instances. Chaos Kong simulates entire region outage. Latency Monkey injects network delays. WHY: proves your failover actually works, not just in theory but in practice. Finds weaknesses before real outages expose them. IMPLEMENTATION: start in staging, gradually move to production. Define 'steady state' (normal metrics), hypothesize what happens during failure, run experiment, observe if system recovers within SLO.

When a component fails, the system continues with reduced functionality rather than total failure. EXAMPLE: if the recommendation engine is down, Amazon still shows the product page — just without 'Customers also bought'. If the cache is down, the system falls back to database (slower but functional). If a non-critical microservice is down, the API returns partial data with a flag indicating degraded mode. IMPLEMENTATION: circuit breakers (see ch13), fallback methods, feature flags to disable failing features.

examples.title: Circuit Breakers in Java & Python
examples.description: To prevent cascading failures, top engineering blogs recommend the Circuit Breaker pattern. It stops requests to a failing service immediately, giving it time to recover rather than overwhelming it.

children.title: Consistency Models
children.summary: Different levels of data consistency guarantees and when to use each in distributed systems.

explanation.overview: When data is replicated across multiple nodes, reads from different nodes may return different values. Consistency models define what guarantees the system provides about what value a read returns.

key_concepts.definition: Every read returns the most recent write, as if there's only one copy of the data. After a write completes, all subsequent reads (from any node) see the new value. HOW: all writes go through a single leader (or consensus protocol like Raft), and reads also go to the leader (or use quorum reads). COST: higher latency (must wait for consensus), lower availability (during partition, CP systems refuse requests). WHEN: financial transactions (bank balance must be accurate), inventory management (must not oversell), user authentication (password change must take effect immediately).

If no new writes occur, eventually all replicas converge to the same value. Reads may return stale data for a window of time (typically milliseconds to seconds). HOW: writes go to any node (or leader), and replicate asynchronously. Reads can go to any node. COST: you may read stale data. BENEFIT: lower latency (no waiting for replication), higher availability (works during partitions). WHEN: social media feeds (seeing a tweet 3 seconds late is fine), DNS (TTL-based propagation), CDN cache (eventually consistent with origin). IMPLEMENTATION: Dynamo-style databases (Cassandra, DynamoDB) with tunable consistency — write to W nodes, read from R nodes. If W + R > N, you get strong consistency. If not, eventual.

If operation A causally precedes operation B (B depends on A's result), then every node sees A before B. Unrelated operations can be seen in any order. EXAMPLE: User posts a photo (A), then comments on it (B). B causally depends on A. Every reader must see the photo before the comment. But another user's unrelated post (C) can appear in any order relative to A and B. HOW: use vector clocks or Lamport timestamps to track causal ordering. Each message carries a logical clock that recipients use to order operations. COST: more complex than eventual, less expensive than strong. Used by: MongoDB (causal consistency sessions).

A user always sees their own writes. After you update your profile picture, you must see the new picture on refresh (even if other users temporarily see the old one). IMPLEMENTATION: route the user's reads to the same replica they wrote to (using sticky sessions or a 'recent write' flag that routes to the leader for a short window after writes).

Once a user sees a value at time T, they never see an older value on subsequent reads. Without this, a user might see their feed at 10:00 AM, refresh and see it at 9:55 AM (reading from a lagging replica), then refresh again and see 10:00 AM. IMPLEMENTATION: pin the user to a specific replica (sticky sessions) or track the user's last-seen timestamp and only serve from replicas at least as fresh.

examples.title: Implementing Tunable Consistency (Quorum Read) in Python
examples.description: How a masterless distributed database (like Cassandra) resolves conflicts during a Read operation when W + R > N.
examples.code:
import asyncio

# Simulating network calls to 3 replicas (N=3)
async def fetch_from_replica(replica_id, key):
    # Returns (value, vector_clock_timestamp)
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    # Simulating divergent state: replica 3 has stale data
    if replica_id == 3:
        return {"value": "old_state", "ts": 100}
    return {"value": "new_state", "ts": 105}

async def quorum_read(key, R=2):
    # Fire requests to all 3 replicas, but we only wait for R (2) responses
    tasks = [fetch_from_replica(i, key) for i in range(1, 4)]
    
    # asyncio.as_completed yields results as they arrive
    responses = []
    for coro in asyncio.as_completed(tasks):
        result = await coro
        responses.append(result)
        if len(responses) == R:
            break # Short-circuit once we satisfy the Read Quorum!
            
    # Conflict Resolution: Return the response with the highest timestamp (LWW)
    best_response = max(responses, key=lambda x: x['ts'])
    print(f"Read Quorum satisfied. Winning value: {best_response['value']}")
    return best_response['value']

asyncio.run(quorum_read('user:123', R=2))

advanced_tweaks.when_to_use: When you need tunable consistency. Read/Write nodes (R/W) must overlap: W + R > N (Total Replicas).
advanced_tweaks.how: If N=3, W=2, R=2 ensures strong consistency because every Read checks at least 2 nodes, guaranteeing it sees the latest write (which hit at least 2 nodes).

examples.title: Consensus Implementations in The Wild
examples.description: When building distributed locks or leader election, don't write your own Consensus algorithm. Developer blogs scream: 'Use existing libraries!'
examples.code:

- Python: rraft-py (Python bindings for the hyper-fast Rust tikv/raft-rs crate) or PyRaftLog for pure Python implementations.
- Go: Hashicorp Raft (used in Consul and Nomad, extremely production hardened).

children.title: Distributed Systems Evaluation Checklist & Decision Matrices
children.summary: A rubric-based checklist to evaluate the fault tolerance and scalability of your distributed architecture.

explanation.overview: Before presenting your final architecture to the interviewer, run it through this mental checklist to catch common distributed systems design flaws.

key_concepts.definition: If the database goes down for 5 seconds and 10,000 requests stack up, what happens when it comes back online? Without Jitter and Exponential Backoff, the system will immediately crash again.
If the network cable between AZ-1 and AZ-2 is cut, does the system halt entirely, or does it degrade gracefully (serve stale data from cache)?

examples.title: Decision Matrix: Scaling Strategy
examples.description: How to choose between vertical and horizontal scaling during an interview.
examples.code:
SCENARIO                          | SCALE STRATEGY | WHY
----------------------------------|----------------|------------------------------------------
100,000 DAU MVP App               | Vertical       | Cheaper, simpler, fits on one strong server.
Stateless API Gateway layer       | Horizontal     | Trivially parallelizable behind an LB.
Stateful Relational Database      | Vertical First | Sharding a relational DB is an absolute last resort.
Background Job Queue Processing   | Horizontal     | Consumer groups easily scale horizontally.
